extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of literature interested in Gabriel García Márquez and magical realism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for producing or analysing prose in the manner of Gabriel García Márquez, focused on stylistic choices (tone, omission, magical realism) and recurring themes/settings (solitude, Macondo, la violencia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Style determined by subject and mood
rubrics_metrics.description: "One doesn't choose the style. ... the style is determined by the subject, by the mood of the times."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate and try to discover the best style for a theme, but avoid forcing an unsuitable style — "If you try to use something that is not suitable, it just won't work." Critics may theorize later, but the author responds primarily to the subject and local way of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit seemingly important details to engage the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: García Márquez was noted for leaving out seemingly important details and events so the reader is forced into a more participatory role in the story development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In No One Writes to the Colonel the main characters are not given names. This practice is influenced by Greek tragedies where important events occur off-stage and are left to the audience's imagination — use strategic omission to invite reader inference rather than filling every gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use off-stage events and namelessness (Greek-tragedy influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Influenced by Greek tragedies (e.g., Antigone, Oedipus Rex) in which important events occur off-stage and are left to the audience's imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactically leave crucial events or identities unshown/unnamed to create resonance and mystery, trusting the reader to supply meaning rather than spelling everything out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounded realism in early works: reflect social reality
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nobody Writes to the Colonel, In Evil Hour, and Big Mama's Funeral all reflect the reality of life in Colombia and this theme determines the rational structure of the books."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use realistic depiction of local social, political, and economic conditions to shape narrative structure and coherence; early García Márquez shows premeditated literature offering a rational framework rooted in Colombia's reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan treatment of the extraordinary
rubrics_metrics.description: "the most frightful, the most unusual things are told with the deadpan expression".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present supernatural or bizarre events in a flat, matter-of-fact tone so that the extraordinary reads as part of ordinary reality. Example: a character ascending physically and spiritually into heaven while hanging laundry in One Hundred Years of Solitude is narrated without rhetorical astonishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine the fantastic and the realistic (magical realism / marvellous realm)
rubrics_metrics.description: The style fits in the 'marvellous realm' and was labeled as magical realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interweave marvelous elements with realistic contexts so the reader accepts the fantastic as an integrated part of the world; avoid exoticizing the magic — treat the marvelous as plausible within the story's reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological suppleness rather than exoticizing magic
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative to a dichotomous view of magic realism: "what is really at stake is a psychological suppleness which is able to inhabit unsentimentally the daytime world while remaining open to the promptings of those domains which modern culture has ... necessarily marginalised or repressed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a psychological openness that can represent everyday life unsentimentally while allowing marginalized, repressed or liminal experiences to surface — the technique privileges interior/psychological coherence over mere stylistic exoticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure magic is grounded in underlying social reality
rubrics_metrics.description: García Márquez and Plinio Apuleyo Mendoza: European readers "are usually aware of the magic of your stories but fail to see the reality behind it.... their rationalism prevents them seeing that reality isn't limited to the price of tomatoes and eggs."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using magical elements, make sure they illuminate or arise from deeper social, cultural, or historical realities so the magic reads as meaningful commentary rather than decorative oddity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore solitude as a central thematic preoccupation
rubrics_metrics.description: The theme of solitude runs through much of García Márquez's works; e.g., Love in the Time of Cholera "explores the solitude of the individual and of humankind...portrayed through the solitude of love and of being in love."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center narratives on individual and collective experiences of solitude; use relationships, love, and social isolation as lenses for broader human and continental conditions (e.g., "Solitude of Latin America").

rubrics_metrics.name: Macondo as a flexible, mythic setting (state of mind)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Macondo is not so much a place as a state of mind, which allows you to see what you want, and how you want to see it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a setting that evokes a particular cultural/regional resonance without strict geographic specificity so it reads both local and universal — use familiar regional markers (Caribbean coastline, Andean hinterland) but leave other elements unspecified to capture a general regional myth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberately non-specific locales to capture regional myth
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when stories do not take place in Macondo, there is often still a consistent lack of specificity to the location ... in accordance with García Márquez's evident attempt to capture a more general regional myth rather than give a specific political analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor evocative, archetypal geography over precise cartography when the aim is to evoke mythic or collective experience rather than detailed political commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtle portrayal of political violence and social disintegration (la violencia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout his novels there are subtle references to la violencia (a brutal civil war). Characters live under unjust situations like curfew, press censorship, and underground newspapers; works like In Evil Hour show "fragmented portrayal of social disintegration provoked by la violencia."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict political trauma indirectly through everyday injustices and social fragments rather than overt polemic; use narrative fragmentation and quotidian detail to imply larger historical violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid polemical propaganda — prioritize literary craft to convey politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Although García Márquez did portray the corrupt nature and the injustices of times like la violencia, he refused to use his work as a platform for political propaganda: "For him, the duty of the revolutionary writer is to write well, and the ideal novel is one that moves its reader by its political and social content, and, at the same time, by its power to penetrate reality and expose its other side."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing politically charged fiction, aim to move and enlighten through craft and narrative depth rather than didactic argument; the ideal political novel reveals complexity and other sides of reality rather than serving as direct propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose richly imagined worlds that reflect continental life and conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Nobel citation: works "in which the fantastic and the realistic are combined in a richly composed world of imagination, reflecting a continent's life and conflicts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build layered, imaginative milieus that synthesize personal, local, and continental histories — ensure that fantastical elements contribute to an expansive vision of society and conflict.
